messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 51
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: School Principal
  trauma_type: Life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 56

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Medical Procedures: Undergoing a medical examination or procedure
  Maladaptive Strategies: Rehearse Conversations: rehearse what to say before any interaction, Isolate Completely: cut off all contact with friends and family, Avoid Medical Cues: Hospitals/ Ambulances/ Physical Examinations
  Memory: Hard to Recall Deliberately: When I try to deliberately remember what happened I find it difficult to access the memory, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

David had always been a man defined by his certainty. As the principal of a bustling middle school, his days were a marathon of decisive action, of calm authority projected in the face of adolescent chaos. He was the one parents and teachers relied on, the steady hand on the tiller. That was before the illness, eighteen months ago. Now, he felt like a stranger inhabiting his own life, a ghost haunting the hallways where he once commanded respect. He looked in the mirror and saw the same 51-year-old man, but the person he had become was unrecognisable to him. He was certain he could no longer rely on himself for even the simplest of tasks.

The collapse had come without warning. One moment he was reviewing budget proposals in his office, the next he was on the floor, a searing pain ripping through his abdomen. The memory, when he dares to approach it, is a chaotic blur. He can’t deliberately recall the sequence of events—the ambulance ride, the emergency room—as a clear narrative. Instead, it exists as visceral fragments. The most potent is the smell. Waking in the ICU, intubated and paralyzed, his first conscious sensation was the overwhelming, chemical sharpness of antiseptic, punctuated by the sting of alcohol swabs on his skin. He couldn’t move, couldn’t speak, couldn’t understand what was happening. He was trapped inside a body that had utterly betrayed him, his back arched against the stiff mattress in a posture of helpless terror.

Now, that terror lives in the air around him. A few months ago, a student scraped her knee on the playground. David walked toward the nurse’s office to check on her and was stopped dead by the faint, clean scent of antiseptic wash wafting from the doorway. He didn’t see the hospital room, but the full emotional intensity of the ICU—the panic, the feeling of suffocation—crashed over him. Without thinking, his back tightened, his hands clenched into fists at his sides, his body reenacting the helpless position he’d been in for days. He turned and fled to his own office, locking the door and fighting for breath.

This constant, lurking threat has reshaped his world. He has come to believe his body is fundamentally unreliable, a ticking time bomb he can no longer trust. This belief dictates his every move. He hasn’t seen a doctor since his hospital discharge, cancelling his last two physicals with flimsy excuses. The very idea of undergoing a medical procedure, of willingly placing his untrustworthy body in the hands of others, is unthinkable. His life has shrunk. He used to have friends, a weekly poker game, but he has cut off all contact. The effort of maintaining a façade of normalcy is too exhausting. After his wife passed away, her sister was his rock; now, her calls go unanswered. It’s easier to be alone than to explain a brokenness he doesn’t understand himself.

Even his work, once his anchor, has become a minefield. Before every staff meeting or parent conference, he now rehearses what he needs to say, sometimes for hours, whispering the words aloud in his empty office. He is terrified that if he doesn’t plan every syllable, his mind will go blank or his body will fail him in front of everyone. The spontaneity and confidence that defined him are gone, replaced by a brittle, carefully constructed performance. The assistant principal, a kind woman named Maria, has started taking on more of his public-facing duties, a quiet shift in responsibility that feels to David like a profound and humiliating failure. It was after he had to ask her to handle the spring open house, unable to face the press of bodies and the potential for unpredictable interactions, that he finally made the call. He sat in his silent home, the quiet amplifying his sense of isolation, and admitted that he could not fix this alone. He doesn't know if the man he was is lost for good, but he is desperate to find a way to trust his own body, and himself, again.
